cues.text: A Prince of the Jagiellonian Dynasty
Born in 1458 in the royal palace at Kraków, Casimir was the second son of King Casimir IV of Poland and grandson of Władysław II Jagiełło, the ruler who had brought Christianity to Lithuania.

Placed at age nine under the care of the respected historian and priest Jan Długosz, Casimir showed remarkable piety and seriousness of purpose even as a child, unusual among princes raised amid the luxury of a royal court.
An Unsuccessful Crown
At thirteen, Casimir was offered Hungary’s throne by a faction discontented with King Matthias Corvinus.
Eager to defend Christian Europe against Ottoman advances, he accepted and marched into Hungary.
The expedition failed when Matthias Corvinus retained sufficient support, forcing Casimir to withdraw and return to Poland without gaining the throne.
Governing Poland with Justice
Resuming his studies under Długosz, Casimir was gradually initiated into affairs of state by his father.
When King Casimir IV departed for an extended stay in Lithuania between 1481 and 1483, the young prince governed Poland in his stead.
Even at so young an age, he earned a reputation for conspicuous prudence, fairness, and personal integrity in the exercise of power.
Refusing a Political Marriage
Casimir's father pressed him to marry the daughter of Emperor Frederick III of Germany, a match that would have secured valuable political alliances.
But Casimir, having privately vowed himself to a life of chastity, firmly declined, choosing instead prayer and continence despite dynastic pressure.
A Devotion to Mary
Throughout his short life, Casimir was known for an especially deep devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary, frequently reciting a long Marian hymn.

The hymn was attributed in tradition to St. Bernard of Clairvaux ; a copy was buried with Casimir at his death and became so closely associated with him that it is sometimes called the 'Hymn of St. Casimir.'
Legacy
Casimir died after a prolonged illness at Grodno in 1484 at only twenty-six years old, and was buried in the cathedral at Vilnius.

Canonized in 1521, he became, and remains, the principal patron of Poland and Lithuania, remembered as a prince who, despite every temptation of wealth, power, and royal marriage available to him, chose instead a life of simplicity, chastity, and devotion.
